item.research_question: Can a quaternary equimolar high-entropy alloy (CoCrFeNi) composed of base metals exhibit higher electrochemical hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) activity in acidic solutions than its individual component metals or platinum?
item.material_system: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (equimolar composition: 26.5:23.7:25.0:24.8 Co:Cr:Fe:Ni), compared with pure Co, Cr, Fe, Ni foils, SS304, and Pt electrodes.
item.processing_route: Arc-melting of 99.99+% pure Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni powders in an argon atmosphere on a water-cooled copper hearth with a tungsten electrode; the button was turned over and re-melted multiple times for homogeneity, sliced into wafers (ca. 8 × 5 × 1 mm3) by electrical discharge machining, and mechanically polished with 0.2 μm alumina powder.
item.test_conditions: Electrochemical testing in 0.5 M H2SO4 (pH 0.3) at ambient temperature and pressure; linear sweep voltammetry at 20 mV/s from 0 to −0.7 V; stability tested by cycling between 0 and −0.45 V at 20 mV/s for 1000 cycles (12.5 h); XPS performed in UHV (1 × 10–10 Torr) with O2 dosing up to 1000 L.
key_findings: The CoCrFeNi HEA exhibits an overpotential of only 60 mV relative to Pt for the HER at a current density of 1 mA/cm2 in 0.5 M H2SO4.
The HEA is more active than each of the individual base metals (Co, Cr, Fe, Ni) by 250 mV or more at 1 mA/cm2.
Ni is the most resistant to oxidation among the components; no Ni oxide formation was detected even after 1000 L of O2 exposure in UHV.
Cr oxides form quickly (within 5 L O2) and saturate well below 500 L O2, while Fe and Co saturate around 500 L O2.
The HEA shows high stability with only ca. 0.1 wt % total weight loss after 1000 electrochemical cycles, with no preferential loss of any particular metal.
Theoretical modeling predicts that the HEA surface becomes partially oxidized in acidic solution, with 19 of 36 fcc sites oxidized and 18 open sites populated with H.
The differential binding strength of H on the partially oxidized HEA surface is within ca. 0.1 eV of the Pt(111) value for approximately 55–70% of the open sites.
item.mechanism: The authors propose that upon exposure to ambient O2, the HEA surface becomes nearly fully oxidized except for Ni-rich sites; under cathodic bias in acidic solution, these sites are partially reduced to form a partially oxidized surface where adsorbed O atoms moderate the hydrogen adsorption energy (ΔGH*) to a level close to that of Pt, thereby enhancing HER activity compared to the un-oxidized base metals.
item.limitations: The study notes that no finite-size surface model can uniquely represent the HEA surface and that the theoretical approach uses an approximate surface model; the UHV oxidation experiments do not directly probe surface oxidation in electrochemical settings.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that a small increase in the concentration of Ni could strengthen H adsorption slightly further, making the alloy even more active for HER, and call for a systematic approach to guide the substitution of precious metals with earth-abundant metals using theoretically predicted random alloy compositions.
quotes: the HEA exhibits an overpotential of only 60 mV relative to Pt for the HER at a current density of 1 mA/cm2.

Ni does not show any new peak associated with nickel oxides up to 1000 L O2, and as can be seen in Figure 9, there is no shift in the position of the 2p3/2 peak of Ni even at 1000 L O2, which suggest lack of Ni oxide formation consistent with our calculations.
This is then confirmed through electrochemical testing of the HEA in a 0.5 M aqueous solution of H2SO4.
